# Background

Measuring gene expression as a time series after a change in
environmental conditions is an increasingly popular way to obtain
precise and cost-effective information about how organisms respond. A
single experiment can follow every gene in the genome across many time
points, as in the dense time course of the *Drosophila melanogaster*
innate immune response, which sampled 21 time points after immune
challenge [@schlamp2021]. Time-series RNA-seq is now used across very
different systems, from immune challenge in flies to embryonic
development in pigs and placental development in mice [@nascimento2017;
@vu2022].

A major challenge in analyzing time-series RNA-seq is determining which
genes are actually responding over time. Variance, measured as deviation
from a gene's mean, does not capture a time-dependent response, in which
each time point is correlated with its neighboring time points: a gene
can be highly variable simply because its replicates disagree. Smoothing
expression across time points can reveal this ordered response, but it
discards information about how noisy each gene's expression is between
replicates.

The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), widely used in signal processing,
describes the strength of an ordered time response while still
accounting for noise between measurements. A challenge with SNR is that
the user must define what counts as "signal". Here we define signal as
the variance in expression explained by a polynomial regression on time
(typically of second or third degree) and noise as the residual
variance. We show that this SNR captures the time response, and that the
same regression also describes the *shape* of each gene's response.

The standard next step in a time-series analysis is to group genes with
similar trajectories. Commonly used approaches include k-means and
hierarchical clustering, with or without smoothing or dimension
reduction, and model-based alternatives such as independent component
analysis [@nascimento2017] and Gaussian process mixture models
[@mcdowell2018]. Density-based methods such as HDBSCAN [@campello2013]
go further and explicitly label genes that do not fit any cluster as
outliers, and have been combined with hierarchical co-expression
clustering to resolve compact gene modules [@dyugay2026]. Every
partitioning method, however, is affected by observations that fit no
group: k-means and PCA can be distorted by a small number of outliers
unless they are modeled explicitly [@witten2013], and removing the least
reliable observations before clustering changes the clusters that
HDBSCAN and k-means recover [@yigin2023]. In time-series RNA-seq, the
least reliable observations are genes with little ordered change and
noisy replicates.

We therefore ask whether SNR, computed for each gene *before*
clustering, identifies the genes that clustering methods fail to place,
and whether removing low-SNR genes improves the clusters that remain. We
compare SNR with simpler summaries of gene variability, and test it
against established clustering methods in terms of 1) identifying the
genes with the strongest time-dependent changes in expression, and 2)
describing the typical shapes of expression responses among groups of
genes.

# Results

## Measuring signal-to-noise in time-series RNA-seq data-sets

For each gene we defined **signal** as the variance in expression
explained by a third-degree polynomial regression of read counts on time
point, and **noise** as the residual variance. The signal-to-noise ratio
(SNR) is their ratio, ESS/RSS, computed on the replicate-level counts so
that disagreement between replicates counts as noise.

To show what high and low SNR look like in practice, we drew six genes
at random from the top 10% and six from the bottom 10% of the 7,512
genes in the immune data-set ranked by SNR (@fig-snr-examples). The
high-SNR examples (SNR 1.22 to 12.82) follow clear trajectories over
time: most dip early and then rise steadily toward the end of the time
course, and one peaks sharply around time points 6 to 8. The two
replicates at each time point agree closely. The low-SNR examples (SNR
0.01 to 0.06) move up and down between neighboring time points with no
consistent direction, and their replicates often disagree. Several of
them are also very lowly expressed, with only one or two reads at most
time points, so part of their noise reflects the sampling error of low
read counts.

![Randomly selected genes from the top 10% (blue) and bottom 10% (red)
of the immune dataset by SNR. Points are individual replicates; the line
joins the mean at each timepoint. Panel titles give each gene's SNR; the
y-axis is set separately for each
gene.](snr_examples_per_gene.png){#fig-snr-examples}

## SNR pre-filtering removes the genes that HDBSCAN cannot cluster

Clustering methods such as k-means and hierarchical clustering assign
every gene to a cluster, whether or not its expression follows any of
the cluster shapes. To see how many genes fit no cluster at all, we
clustered the immune trajectories (replicate means, log2(counts + 1),
z-scored within each gene) with HDBSCAN [@campello2013], a density-based
method that labels genes in sparse regions as outliers rather than
forcing them into a cluster, and visualized the result with UMAP
[@mcinnes2018].

Before any filtering by SNR, most genes in the immune data-set do not
fall into a clear group. When all genes were clustered with HDBSCAN
(minPts = 50) and visualized with UMAP (@fig-umap-prefiltered), only two
compact groups of genes formed clusters, while the large majority were
flagged as outliers and spread across the map as a continuous cloud with
no clear boundaries. These outliers are the genes whose relationship to
SNR we examine in the next section.

![UMAP of the immune dataset before SNR filtering, coloured by HDBSCAN
cluster (minPts = 50). Grey points are genes flagged as outliers
(HDBSCAN cluster
0).](images/umap_hdbscan_ImmuneCounts-01.png){#fig-umap-prefiltered}

We then asked which of these genes the SNR filter would remove. Keeping
each gene's label from the unfiltered HDBSCAN run, we removed the 10%,
25% and 50% of genes with the lowest SNR (corresponding to SNR cutoffs
of 0.08, 0.17 and 0.37) and showed the remaining genes on the same UMAP
(@fig-umap-prefilter). The filter removed outliers far more readily than
clustered genes: 80% of outliers versus 19% of clustered genes at the 10
filter, 30% versus 4% at 25%, and 60% versus 12% at 50%. At every
cutoff, the filter removed 5 to 12 times more of the outliers than of
the clustered genes. In the UMAP, the outliers emptied out of the center
of the map as the cutoff rose, while both clusters at its edges stayed
largely intact.

SNR is computed for each gene before any clustering and without
reference to any cluster. That it removes HDBscan's outliers so
preferentially shows that SNR, measured before clustering, identifies
largely the same unreliable genes that HDBSCAN identifies after
clustering.

![The UMAP from @fig-umap-nofilter after removing the 10%, 25% and 50%
of genes with the lowest SNR. Each gene keeps its label from the
unfiltered HDBSCAN run, and genes removed by the filter are hidden, so
the panels show which genes each filter removes. Panel titles give the
percentage of HDBSCAN outliers and of clustered genes
removed.](images/snr_cutoff_umap_hdbscan.png){#fig-umap-prefilter}
